The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$

questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14141831/assets/617a69d44661d03e1c170b0c397d11f6437a7222c286df5023154371ec90ab4d.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(-\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$ 

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14141831/assets/2d50f2375c071d8bfb4c5c58a836bef76a70557c2593d4df9acf48f9f0e7527b.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14141831/assets/98e9c8442c17cbc77083c5dc55a9d74324befa05e3cd47e1c65c38cd510c08c6.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({3}^{4}-{1}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =20[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{2}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =10{[{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =10({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(0)) \\  & =10(1-0) \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =9 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3)}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +9 & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14141831/assets/7515fffda1580baa332df454e7fe53a60f70944215f13d83e0e2269a0101dba6.png)

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
